While the world is structurally mature and violent, the underlying mechanical loop frequently treats the player exactly like that. If you are looking for a true tactical or mental challenge where a failure to think critically carries real consequences, Cyberpunk entirely fails to deliver.

The mental load is practically zero.

[h2]One of the Best RPGs I've Ever Played[/h2]

Baldur's Gate 3 is genuinely one of the best RPGs I've played in years. The amount of freedom and attention to detail is ridiculous, and it's honestly made going back to other RPGs a little difficult.

What impresses me most is just how much the game accounts for. There are so many ways to approach quests, conversations, and encounters that even the most ridiculous ideas sometimes work. You'd think you've found some clever way to break a quest, only to discover that the developers already anticipated it and recorded dialogue specifically for it.

[b]The writing and companions are easily some of the game's strongest points.[/b] The characters actually feel like people with their own personalities, motivations, and problems rather than just followers who exist to carry your junk and occasionally help in combat.

Although, to be fair, travelling with this group would be an absolute nightmare. Everyone has some deeply concerning personal baggage, half of them are keeping secrets, and somehow I'm expected to keep the group functioning when I can barely be trusted to make sensible decisions myself.

The combat is fantastic too. There's an incredible amount of depth to the classes, spells, abilities, and environmental interactions. Experimenting with different builds and party compositions is genuinely enjoyable, and the game gives you plenty of opportunities to get creative.

That being said, nothing quite prepares you for the experience of missing a 95% chance to hit twice in a row.

I know how probability works. Doesn't mean I have to like it.

[b]The replayability is probably what I appreciate most.[/b] Different classes, races, companions, and story decisions can change the experience significantly. Even after finishing a playthrough, there's always another build I want to try, another character I want to create, or a different approach to a quest I'm curious about.

Baldur's Gate 3 has a lot going for it, which is talked about in great detail in other reviews, and I don't need to repeat what they say.  The game is extremely well polished.

What most reviews fail to mention is the game's problems.  The fundamental gameplay basics of the game are just, bad.  Not the game balance; the problems are even more basic than that.  Controls, camera, environmental collision, pathing, physics, ui problems.  Not to mention crashing.  The basic fundamentals of a game which should be ironclad before a game dev has barely done work on graphics or writing a story.

The game is extremely polished, but at core functionality level, the game might as well be a pre-alpha build.

Most people are okay with that, and there are lots of mods that exist that fix some of these problems, several of which I installed.  But I've always been of the opinion that mods should add to a game, not fix the game's code for the developers.

And it leaves a very sour taste in my mouth when I encounter minor glitches every few minutes, in what is otherwise a good game with a good story and compelling characters.

Counter-Strike 2 is not merely a video game. It is a breathtaking fusion of mathematical elegance, economic sophistication, mechanical precision, and digital artistry. Valve has created something so extraordinarily complex and beautiful that calling it a first-person shooter feels almost insulting.

[h2]TL;DR – Not Recommended (Overrated, Falling Short of Promises)[/h2]
[h3]Intro & Context[/h3]
Cyberpunk 2077 has great visuals, fun cyberware customization, and a decent ending, but it falls far short of its pre-launch promises. I often see players calling this game phenomenal, praising its side quests, build variety, combat, writing, and voice acting. Personally, I disagree on almost every front. While the game has its strengths, the gap between what was promised prior to launch and its actual execution falls short. What [i]Cyberpunk 2077[/i] could have been versus what it ended up being are a universe apart.
[h3]1. Shallow Dialogue and the Illusion of Choice[/h3]
To me, the dialogues feel shallow, and the options provided are sometimes plain stupid. For example, V’s tone will jump from a neutral voice to an angry voice and back to neutral, completely predefined by the situation. If a situation is negative and I want to play it positive or neutral, I simply can't. The dialogues are tied strictly to fixed objectives; it feels like the player has a choice, when in reality, they don't. Even when choices are made, there are no real consequences or major differences, as everything converges to the same outcome.
The game ignores player agency even in small details. Smoking and drinking are heavily forced into the story, and you often cannot refuse them. On top of that, the plot suffers from noticeable holes (or poorly explained narratives), such as the Johnny Silverhand helicopter flashback where Rogue says, "Not again," which feels jarring and unexplained.
[h3]2. Wasted Potential in Lifepaths and Narrative[/h3]
The game offers three character origins, so I naturally expected three distinct storylines. Instead, they all revolve around the exact same plot with minimal differences.
In a way, I was disappointed that I couldn't have a more unique experience. I wanted to play V as a true corporate spy. Infiltrating corporations, stealing corpo secrets, engaging in Arasaka

A little while after you escape, a voice inside your head that wasn't there prior to probing starts encouraging you to seek out other probes to shove inside yourself. You now have a choice:

a) listen to all of the information presented to you and attempt deprobing / do not engage with further probing

b) listen to the new voice in your head and continue collecting probes to insert into yourself in exchange for neat magic powers. When you use the probes, a little visual pops up of your brain turning to goo, but don't worry about that.

This is the core conundrum the game presents. Sell your body and soul for power, or abstain. Guess where it leads?

Nowhere. There's no negative outcome for sacrificing your humanity outside of a single pass/fail roll that you can reattempt via save/reload. Your choice to take the game's negative presentation of "probing" at face value actively makes your gameplay less varied by locking yourself out of a useful skill tree, and it has little to no bearing on the trajectory of the plot or the ending you receive.

This is BG3 in a nutshell: a strong opening that stumbles so hard in the final lap that it actively undermines everything that came before.

CS2 is honestly one of the biggest disappointments in the history of competitive gaming.

What happened to Counter-Strike? We went from having CS:GO, a game with personality, competitive integrity, and an incredible community, to this unfinished, frustrating mess called CS2.

Let's talk about the anti-cheat. VAC is an absolute joke. Cheaters are everywhere, blatant hackers can ruin entire matches, and legitimate players are left wasting their time. You can spend thousands of hours improving your aim, movement, and game sense, just to get destroyed by someone using cheats. The competitive experience is pathetic when you can't even trust the integrity of your matches.

Valve seems completely disconnected from its player base. We keep getting skins, cases, and cosmetic content, while one of the most important aspects of the game remains neglected: ACTUALLY STOPPING CHEATERS.

CS:GO had problems, but at least it felt like Counter-Strike. It had character, atmosphere, and an identity. CS2 feels like a soulless replacement that nobody asked to experience in this state. Source 2 was supposed to be an upgrade, but what did we really gain? Better graphics? For what, if the actual gameplay experience is constantly ruined?

The game that once represented competitive excellence now feels like an endless cycle of frustration:
- Useless anti-cheat against blatant cheaters.
- Unfair and frustrating matchmaking.
- A community losing patience.
- Updates that don't address the biggest problems.
- Valve prioritizing monetization while fundamental issues remain.

The most insulting part is that Counter-Strike has an enormous budget, a massive player base, and one of the most successful competitive gaming communities in history. Yet players still have to beg for basic competitive integrity.

CS2 isn't the evolution of CS:GO. It feels like a downgrade wearing a new coat of paint.

As a budget-conscious gamer, I don't buy games often. Every purchase needs to justify its existence, so I was honestly super skeptical before pulling the trigger on this.
Oh boy, was I wrong. Baldur’s Gate 3 isn't just worth every single penny—it is a full-blown existential threat to your sleep schedule.

The Good:
Value for money / Absolute Black Hole of Time: Calling this game "long" is an understatement. You can sink 50 hours into it, feel like you've lived an entire lifetime, and then realize you haven't even made a dent in the main story.

Turn-based combat: I usually avoid turn-based games (I’m strictly an action/RPG person), but if every turn-based game were built like BG3, I’ve been living under a rock. The combat is addictively fun.

Actual choices: I love choice-driven games (Telltale's The Walking Dead, Dispatch, Oxenfree), but BG3 makes them look like child's play. Even the most minor, throwaway decision can completely derail or reshape your narrative. The sheer freedom to act like a saint or an unhinged chaos goblin is unmatched.

The Bad:
It will ruin your real life: I literally had to force myself to stop playing because my actual responsibilities were collapsing around me. I survived on a solid 4 hours of sleep a night for a week straight because "just one more turn" turned into sunrise every single night.

Verdict: A genuine D&D masterpiece. 10/10, would ruin my real-life functioning to play it again.

Conversations can collapse into combat without warning. The game withholds information under the guise of tension when it's actually just poor player communication. To avoid repeating what has been already written pretty much everywhere on the internet, I'll tell what has been my personal experience with this game:
I began playing this together with a friend - and I hated it: the main characters sounded annoying, borderline hostile to me. I felt that they were a burden.
I knew nothing about this game, didn't even watch the trailers.
I thought that just like CP2077 the whole story was going to be about getting rid of some magic worm that has been put in my brain and that it would be over soon.
I left the game in the middle of Act 1 and then I started a new, fresh run: this time, I listened more carefully to my companions, and only asked questions when I felt that they were ready to talk.
197 hours later, I miss all of them. It's a sensation that I have not felt in years, maybe decades: missing a fictional character from a book or a TV series.
You may think that this is just a fantasy game, but it's inspired by life and teaches you about love and friendship... with a lot of battle strategy on top 🤭
Sometimes I think that there will never be a game like this again.
But, maybe in 10 years, another group of talented people will look at what Larian did here and say: let's make a sequel. And I really hope that I will be there to play it!
Huge thanks to Larian and to all the people who worked on this game.

Act 1: Absolutely amazing. The absolute peak of RPG gaming.

Act 2: Still good, but the cracks are starting to show.

Act 3: An incomprehensible clusterfuck where everything pretends to matter, but somehow nothing feels particularly impactful anymore.

Baldur's Gate 3 starts off as one of the most incredible RPG experiences I've ever had. Act 1 is genuinely fantastic. The exploration, the companions, the choices, the feeling that you're just a bunch of adventurers trying to make sense of the world around you. It's everything I want from an RPG.

Act 2 is still good, but things start feeling increasingly railroaded. Misinterpret one little thing, make a decision without fully understanding its consequences, and suddenly something massive happens that can sour the rest of your campaign. Player agency starts feeling less like freedom and more like trying to guess what the writers intended you to do.

And then comes Act 3.

Good lord, what happened here?

Suddenly you're drowning in supposedly world-shattering revelations, grand conspiracies, and characters with increasingly ridiculous ambitions. Everything is presented as the most important thing imaginable, yet very little of it actually feels meaningful.

It's like starting out reading The Fellowship of the Ring, embarking on this wonderful, grounded adventure with a group of companions, only for the story to slowly transform into some American Gods-style drama where the biggest, strongest, most important beings in existence all have the biggest, meanest plans.

And of course, you and your merry band of increasingly overpowered superheroes are the only ones who can stop them.

Somewhere along the way, the grounded RPG adventure turns into a comical superhero flick.

And perhaps the funniest part is that, in doing so, Baldur's Gate 3 stays remarkably faithful to D&D 5e.

Because it suffers from exactly the same progression problem: you start out as a bunch of nobodies worrying about goblins stealing someone's chickens

This was a difficult disapproval to write, but I stand by it.

First the good: 

Cyberpunk is a compelling story. It explores deep topics like identity, human nature, and autonomy in new innovative ways. It fleshes out its world and memorable characters in ways that will stay with you. In between that chaotic action, it surprises you with touching moments (I might have cried at a certain persons funeral, which felt real, organic, and personal).

Cyberpunk is a good RPG: lots of customization options, builds, equipment progression, housing options.

Now the bad:

Cyberpunk is didactic (designed to impart some doctrine of morality or philosophy). It wears its ideology on its sleeves, and leaves the player almost no agency to take a different perspective, until the very end, and even then the game punishes you harshly for disagreeing. Characters will often tell you what you believe, like when Takamura complains that you blame corporations for everything. I, the human, understand that human nature is to blame, and corporations as just a vehicle for it. But V does not. To play this game, you must accept that you are simply watching a characters story, rather than being the character.

Plotholes that ruin the endings. This ties into my earlier comment that the game punishes you for disagreeing with its anti-corporate ideology. The punishments, which I wont spoil here, seem to be injected artificially, rather than the natural result of V's decision. And this extends to other people: others will suffer, even though the result is completely illogical and unrelated to V's decision. While in other endings, they have better outcomes, even though that is also unrelated to the decisions. The devs make it very clear that disagreeing with their worldview is not OK.

Finally, CDProjectRED irritates me by pretending to be pro-mods, while they post no public API docs for modders, forcing them to reverse engineer the engine. By this, I mean that there is no public interface for modding

There are many things wrong with Cyberpunk 2077 fundamentally. This review covers the base game up to update 2.0. It had MANY issues at launch and was the worst launch of a game this size in modern times without exception, on both PC and Console (Sony offered full refunds just after release). Let’s put that aside and give it the benefit of the doubt on its current state (without the DLC), despite those issues and the lies told by CDPR, though those lies will be mentioned where the game is lacking.

I tried to replay it for the 2.0 update. It now has a 2.5 update adding lots of visual customization (clothes, hair styles, cybernetic colours), a side-quest tied in with the new anime, a new radio station, a perk to dual wield power category handguns, and new tarot cards to discover plus QOL updates. I haven’t tried these, but such small changes can’t fix the game’s issues, so this review focuses on the main game.

Writing & Choices:
The writing is terrible. At the start you choose Nomad, Corpo or Streetkid. None of them matter, and I don’t mean in the end; they stop mattering 30 minutes in, apart from a few extra dialogue options before Konpeki Plaza. V has the same vocal delivery whether he’s a fancy Corpo in a suit, a Nomad in the desert or a Streetkid in Night City. It’s jarring when you pick Corpo and V talks like he’s chilling at a bar instead of actually fitting the role. He could be more stoic or conniving, but he’s the same from start to end with the same delivery on all lines. I can’t remember one memorable line V said in the whole game.

The futuristic slang is heavy handed. The idea seems to be that if enough is thrown at you, you’ll feel pulled into the universe, but it’s so overt that you get sick of the filler terms. It doesn’t feel natural, and you can practically hear the VAs enunciate these weird words at a slower pace because they just don’t feel normal to say. The real life equivalent would be Toronto slang.

I'm genuinely baffled that people consider this a masterpiece.

I played Cyberpunk at launch. It was terrible. Six years later, with all the updates, I've given it another proper chance. Somehow, I'm just as disappointed.

Night City is an enormous, lifeless film set. The NPCs are glorified scenery. They wander around aimlessly, barely interact with their surroundings and react to danger like pedestrians from GTA 3. Compare that with KCD2, where people actually have jobs, routines and lives of their own.

The main characters are barely any better. V is dull, everyone seems desperate to be edgy, and constant swearing doesn't make dialogue interesting. I genuinely couldn't care less what these characters have to say.

The combat is tedious. Bullet-sponge enemies, clumsy shooting, awful scripted encounters and embarrassingly basic stealth.

And the endless forced sequences for what is meant to be an open world game. Walk here. Watch this. Crawl along the floor holding W. Sit through another conversation. I've spent more time skipping forced dialogue because i just don't care about anything that is being forced on me. For a supposedly open-world RPG, it seems remarkably determined to stop me from actually playing.

Even the much-praised graphics don't impress me. Fancy lighting can't disguise a world that feels artificial and strangely lifeless.

I absolutely loved The Witcher 3, RDR2, both Kingdom Come games, Baldur's Gate, Disco Elysium. I love slow, character-driven RPGs with meaningful dialogue and immersive worlds.
Cyberpunk has somehow made me resent all of those things.

It's tedious, boring and relentlessly scripted. It mistakes cinematic presentation for good storytelling and visual detail for a living world.

Six years later, I still don't understand the praise. It is terrible.

If you've played dark souls then you know what you're getting into. For the rest of us:
Yes it's a huge world, with gorgeous scenery. But the roleplaying elements are paltry. (Do you want to marry this woman you just met? Yes or no.) The music is barebones. What little story you get is cryptic and obtuse. While the open world is nice for progression at your own pace, it's not a crowded or lively world. The few NPCs seem more interested in insulting you, I suppose to mirror the relentless barrage of combat.

At the end of the day, it's just a dressed up game about boss fights. The other enemies are pathetic in comparison, and they don't train you for the boss fight. If you aren't willing to try a boss 5-20 times in a row then it will be frustrating. And then they ruin it by shoving you in a tiny room with multiple enemies. Not much beyond the basics is explained in detail so you will have to do too much research. I found the console interface to be lacking, the weapon and build choices to be irrelevant (They all have quite similar speed). The way animations lock your character(including flinching) just feels cumbersome and negated the fun of this game for me. If you play ~perfectly~, then it feels good-- it's an abusive style. The horseback combat did add a nice variety. None of the fancy weapons or modifiers or craftables matter as much as rolling at the correct time. It's just a game about rolling. Spare yourself the frustration and just watch someone else play for the scenery.

The Persona 5 of Souls: Beautiful art and fluid movement can’t hide that deliberate combat mastery was traded for mass market spectacle, serving up hollow power fantasies disguised as punishing depth.

The 500-Hour Fallacy: Spare me the "you got your money's worth" routine. Thoroughly testing builds and exploring the map across hundreds of hours doesn't excuse a back third that collapses under recycled encounters and artificial stat bloat. Walking away before the credits wasn't an act of rage or burnout, it was realizing the game had completely run out of ideas and stopped respecting my time.

Refusal to Support PC: Still no native ultra-wide support out of the box for a flagship release. Rendering the extra viewport only to deliberately mask it with black bars on modern monitors is lazy.

Shallow Cashgrabs: I never planned on reviewing this game, but the Tarnished Pack sealed the deal. Even as a Dark Souls II defender, it's blatant, low effort nostalgia bait. Blaming Bandai Namco lets FromSoftware off the hook for building it, and buying into cosmetic nickel and diming signals to both that standards no longer matter.

If you are reading this, then you probably already know the positives of Baldur’s Gate 3: freedom of choice, great voice acting, strong quest design, memorable companions, and the ridiculous amount of ways you can solve problems. I'm not going to sit here and pretend those things are not impressive, because they are.

But because those parts have already been praised to death, I want to focus on what, in my opinion, makes the game overrated.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is clearly a good game, but I don’t think it is the flawless masterpiece people make it out to be. To me, it is also bloated, clunky, awkward, weirdly horny, and surprisingly weak when it comes to the feeling of progression. I will address each of those in the following sections.

[h2]Weak Progression[/h2]

One of my biggest problems with BG3 is progression. For such a huge RPG, I rarely felt genuinely excited about my character becoming stronger.

The story moves forward, the stakes get bigger, and the locations become more dramatic, but my actual character build often felt weirdly static. Gear progression especially felt underwhelming. It is very possible to find strong equipment in Act 1 and keep using it through Act 2 and even into Act 3.

I understand that this is probably good for balance, as it avoids the usual RPG problem where every item becomes useless after two hours. But from a player perspective, it can feel boring. You defeat major enemies, explore dangerous areas, open some impressive-looking chest, and then the reward is something you instantly send to camp because your old gear is still better.

I mean there is clearly something wrong when I'm deep into Act 3 and still wearing gear from Act 1 without feeling much reason to replace it. Loot should be exciting. I should look at a new weapon, armour piece, ring, or cloak and think, "Oh, this changes my build." But too often in BG3, loot just feels like mildly interesting clutter.

A great D&D adaptation, but a frustrating game

Baldur’s Gate 3 does an impressive job of translating D&D rules into a video game. Character classes, spells, abilities, dice rolls and many other mechanics are remarkably well implemented.

Unfortunately, I increasingly dislike the actual game built around those mechanics.

The biggest problem is the combat design. Especially in Act 3, major encounters constantly introduce enemies with special abilities that are poorly explained or completely unexpected. Enemies become invisible, stun characters, move without provoking opportunity attacks, apply multiple status effects, create darkness, and use combinations of actions that are difficult to understand from the player's perspective.

The problem isn't difficulty. **The problem is a lack of information.**

A good D&D encounter gives you enough information to make tactical decisions. BG3 too often makes you discover the rules by getting hit by them first. Eventually combat starts feeling less like *“How do I outsmart these enemies?”* and more like *“What ridiculous special ability did the game just pull out of nowhere?”*

Large encounters are another problem. Watching 15–20 enemies take their turns one after another makes fights incredibly slow. Combine that with all the status effects, animations and special abilities, and some battles become an exhausting exercise in waiting.

The camp system also becomes increasingly annoying. Wanting to take a long rest can turn into another cutscene, companion conversation, romance scene, dream sequence or even a fight. The companions are interesting, but the game sometimes feels like **group therapy with occasional adventuring in between**.

Loot has the opposite problem. In BG1 and BG2, finding a magical item was exciting. In Act 3 of BG3, I constantly find supposedly powerful items and think: *“What am I supposed to do with this?”* Many are so build-specific that they immediately become vendor trash.

Firstly, let's get this out of the way: Souls fans, this review is not for you. You already bought the game, completed it six times and are busily posting a long rant nobody will read about why whatever weapon is underrated/overpowered. 

For the rest of us, who might dip in and out of Souls games from time to time: this is just a Souls game but worse. The only thing that makes it any different from Dark Souls 1, 2, 3 or any other Fromsoft game is the open world - and the open world makes literally everything worse. 

Don't get me wrong - it was the correct decision to put an open world in. The game isn't for me, it's for the Souls fans who've played every game FromSoft release a dozen times over and just need something new. For those people, the open world is the least harmful breath of fresh air possible. 

If you're not sick of the sight of Souls games, though, the open world is a terrible addition. Pacing is dead and buried, the usually stellar map design is relegated to only existing in dungeons, and you have no idea where you're supposed to go next. If you don't look it up you can guarantee you'll miss a region entirely, then have to choose between never experiencing it or doing it while horribly overlevelled. [b]tl;dr[/b] - Many times I've regretted giving this game chances. Turn back... unless you're a masochist. 

Buy only at deep discount if you're a CRPG fan. Accolades and the community's abusive attachment disorder aside, this is a still painfully janky game three years after release. It's not terrible, but... if you're bothered by poor UX or bugs, prepare to suffer death by a thousand little cuts.

[h2][b]The UI - frenemy at best:[/b][/h2]

*  The default camera constantly gets in the way. At times it's so disorienting you'll struggle to tell what's going on. Just to attack somebody the game keeps obscuring, you'll have to click this over here... then that over there... then that up there...(By Act 2 I had to install a mod just to make it playable).

* In a game where every other threat triggers turn based mode, do traps? Nope. Command low level parties perishing on the clock as you frantically try to button-press your way out of it. Worse - press wrong, and it's possible to start dialogue between characters _while they burn in real time_. Like some dark comedy, party locked behind a text based UI, you discuss whatever plot point Larian felt more important than characters gradually cooking into charcoal briquettes, their screams punctuating your mouse clicks.

*  Try to shoot a pesky goblin who hit you just a moment before and you begin a new mini-game: line-of-sight-wackamole. Spend many mouse clicks sleuthing exactly which spot will allow you to satisfy vague yet simultaneously strict conditions without yourself stumbling through acid, poison, or fire. Don't worry, when you give up, the auto-aim is still there to push you through things that hurt.

[h2][b]Bugs - so many still awkward or outright broken features:[/b][/h2]

*  Group pathing is excellent... at doing exactly the wrong thing. Click to go around or even jump over that obviously dangerous acid pool, and your party members follow you... stumbling through it like idiots anyway. Break group to avoid this?

Given how hyped this game is, I would like to give you an in-depth analysis of both its positive and negative aspects and explain to you why I don’t recommend Baldur’s Gate 3 for most players. I will break this review down into the Good, the Bad and the Ugly:

The Good:
Let’s start with what makes this game truly shine.
Characters. You’ll get up to 10 recruitable companions with lots of unique dialogues and (for the most part) their own personal quests, some of which fantastically written, revealing rich origin stories including deep character development. Add stellar voice acting on top of all that and you get a highly immersive and memorable experience! 
Motion capture animations. Another reason why this game and its characters are so immersive is the motion capture animations. I think I’ve never experienced so many characters in a single video game coming so vividly and iconically to life as in bg3. Again, the voice acting adds massively to that.
Adjusting Dungeons & Dragons rules. For those of you who are unfamiliar with the original pen and paper game, it’s extremely unbalanced, especially when comparing the different classes to play. In the community, it’s widely known that there is a huge power gap between spellcaster and martial classes which gradually widens from middle to late levels. Larian studios apparently learned from DnD players homebrewing and elegantly solved this by cutting the maximum level down to 12 (which is btw how most tabletop DnD campaigns are being played) and redesigning certain classes.
Soundtrack. It’s all you could ask for in an RPG: epic during intense moments, soft during emotional moments, dreamy during exploration and overall fantastical.

The Bad:
As cool and amazing as the good stuff sounds, there is a lot of bad stuff we need to address here.

**Elden Ring – Ein gutes Souls-like, aber kein gutes Open-World-Spiel**

Die Open World von Elden Ring überzeugt mich nicht. Es fehlt ein Questlog, NPCs sind teilweise kaum wiederzufinden, und ihre Dialoge geben oft zu wenig Hinweise darauf, wie ihre Quests weitergehen. Erst im dritten Durchlauf konnte ich Rannis Quest vollständig abschließen. Dass man für solche Quests teilweise externe Guides benötigt, empfinde ich als schlechtes Questdesign.

Abseits der Bosskämpfe gibt es für mich wenig, was die offene Welt wirklich interessant macht. Katakomben und Bergwerke bieten gelegentlich spannende Erkundung, aber vieles andere fühlt sich wie Beschäftigungstherapie an, um den Charakter für die nächsten Bosskämpfe vorzubereiten. Die eigentliche Geschichte bleibt dabei erstaunlich banal: Man besiegt mächtige Gegner, um selbst Eldenfürst zu werden.

Die Bosskämpfe sind dagegen anspruchsvoll, fordernd und teilweise hervorragend gestaltet. Hier liegen die größten Stärken des Spiels. Die Kämpfe verlangen Geduld, Ausdauer und die Bereitschaft, aus Fehlern zu lernen.

**Mein Fazit:** Elden Ring ist für mich ein sehr gutes Souls-like, aber kein überzeugendes Open-World-Spiel. Die offene Welt wirkt eher wie ein Mittel zum Zweck, um die Bosskämpfe miteinander zu verbinden. Wer herausfordernde Bosskämpfe liebt, kommt auf seine Kosten. Wer eine gut erzählte Geschichte, nachvollziehbare Quests und eine lebendige Open World erwartet, wird dagegen enttäuscht.

When you see the negative reviews from people like me with hundreds and thousands of hours of playtime, that's your signal that something happened. Something went wrong. 
Elden Ring is a masterpiece of a game with excellent story telling and visuals. It's a piece of art that I intend to continue to share with as many people as I can because good art deserves to be seen. So why the negative. 
FromSoftwares parent company recently had a shift in power via a stock buy from a company who has shown anticonsumer interests in the past. These may not be the exact details, and in any other game this would be not the most egregious addon on offer. But this is the first of it's kind in a fromsoft title. It's a canary so to speak. What is more important to me is the history of the addon itself. The addon was a way to move copies for the switch 2. This extra content was exclusive to the switch 2 for a period and is now being allowed to branch out to the other versions. Which is fine, that's how business works. The problem, however, is that the switch 2 copy of elden ring is the exact same price as the shadow of the erdtree bundle. Meaning switch 2 has the new addon content, the dlc, and the base game for 79.99. Everyone else is the ONLY ONES footing the "bill" for this addon content.

Highly Rated, But a Tedious and Punishing Trial-and-Error Experience
Rating: Not Recommended
If you are buying this game based on its glowing masterwork reviews, hoping for a smooth and immersive fantasy RPG adventure to relax with after work, you should think twice.
1. Extremely Vague and Frustrating Mission Guidance
The quest design offers little to no clear directional guidance. Instead of rewarding exploration, the system leaves you to blindly fumble around huge maps. This lack of structure leads to aimless wandering rather than any real sense of discovery.
2. Punishing Invisible Traps and Chain-Aggro Mechanics
What is often praised as "unrivaled freedom" is actually a hyper-fussy physical and rule simulator. Simply walking over to inspect an area can trigger beast aggression, call over guards, and sound alarm drums—instantly turning an entire encampment hostile and forcing a GAME OVER. A single misstep can wipe out tens of minutes or hours of progress, creating immense frustration.
3. Tedious Micro-Management and Fractured Combat
The combination of mandatory turn-based combat and complex D&D rules makes every action feel like solving a math problem. Party members frequently unlink or get stuck behind terrain, requiring constant, tedious micromanagement. The combat lacks fluid feedback and feels more like administrative homework than rewarding gameplay.
Summary:
This game may appeal to hardcore players who have endless free time to study tabletop rulebooks and enjoy trial-and-error reloading. However, for players seeking a fluid, enjoyable fantasy adventure with direct positive feedback, playing this is simply an exercise in frustration.

FromSoft continues their storytelling style, which is to say vague, abstruse, and limited, with little in the way of player character motivations to be doing anything that you’re doing. To be frank, we got more world building from the 4 minute story trailer that came out three years before the game than we actually got in the game itself. The quest design continues to suck with NPCs declining to tell you where they will be going next in order to continue their quests, and usually declining to give you names of places to go when telling you what to do. If you want to complete most of the quests in the game, you will likely need to look up the steps online. FromSoft is a big AAA studio at this point, so there is little excuse for the continued poor storytelling and quest design. They proved with Sekiro that they can create compelling plots and characters while still leaving a lot up to player interpretation. Sekiro kept the good parts about the writing and world building of the Souls games and excised the bad. Unfortunately, FromSoft regressed with Elden Ring. [b]Cyberpunk 2077[/b] has an incredible amount of potential, but I struggle to understand how such an interesting universe can feel so average in its execution. I first tried it in 2020 and disliked almost everything, from the story to the gameplay. Returning several years later, I can recognise the improvements, but many fundamental problems remain. Night City is beautiful, its architecture and visual design are impressive, and the universe has enormous potential. Unfortunately, a beautiful city filled with NPCs does not automatically become a living world.

One of my biggest problems is how superficial the world feels. Too many NPCs exist simply to fill the streets. Most stand around doing practically nothing, staring into the distance or repeating basic animations. You occasionally see characters talking, but these interactions rarely develop into anything meaningful. I am not asking for every NPC to have a complex routine or storyline. I mean basic everyday life: people interacting, recognising familiar faces, following routines and reacting naturally. Night City should feel like a place that exists independently of the player. Instead, it feels like a backdrop. Fewer NPCs with meaningful interactions would have been better than streets full of characters that barely do anything.

Other open-world games handle this better. The Witcher 3 makes Geralt feel connected to the world, with people recognising him as a mutant. Bethesda games also use conversations and NPC reactions to acknowledge the player's presence and actions. In Skyrim, even a bard singing about your achievements makes your progress feel relevant. Cyberpunk rarely creates that connection. Mission characters may know V is a mercenary, but the rest of the world barely acknowledges who you are or what you have accomplished. I've debated with myself a lot if I should give this game a good or bad review, because in many ways it's a really great game, but the issues I have with the game is so core to the experience that I simply can't justify a good review.

The bad:
 - When you do an attack it attacks in the direction of your last movement input. I believe it should attack in the direction of where you're looking.
 - Dodge and run on the same key. This makes a lot of the dodging so inconsistent since it's very obvious that starting to run is very delayed, and if you're already running it suddenly require you to unclick + click to dodge.
 - Action buffering seems *very* inconsistant. I've have yet to figure out the exact rules for when an action buffers, and when it doesn't. Because of this most often the action buffering will get me killed, because my char will do unpredicable actions I didn't expect.
 - Poisen/rot/etc. swamps seems to only make you stand in a corner and wait and waste your IRL time mostly.
 - Hotbar and menus in general just seem so badly designed. Hotbar/weapon swaps require you as a mouse user to let go of your mouse to do the swaps.
 - Many bosses 2nd stage seems to use *spam particles on players screen so he can't see* as a difficulty mechanic.
 - Area denial attacks from many bosses seems to have very bad hurt boxes.

The good:
 - Stunning game.
 - Great and rewarding boss design.
 - Insane amount of hours of content (granted 75% of that is dying fighting bosses).

Overall:
I really enjoyed the game in general, but because the attack/movement mechanics is just such a core part of the game, the frustration with the bad control design in the end means I'll be giving the game a negative review.

Having played both Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 to death, and loving every moment of it, I was severely disappointed in how they handled its nominal successor.

-Not being able to pause, ever, citing "you don't need to!" as their reason (it's usually true, but absolutely not 100% so).
-When engaged in conversation with a person or an object, it's *always* the character initiating the conversation (on purpose or by accident) that does the skill check, regardless of how (un)realistic it would be for them to do so (here they could have learned a ton from the creators of the Pathfinder games)
-Time only being counted through long rests makes the game less immersive
-Inventory handling is a mess
-Being able to teleport items to your camp is unimmersive
-Being able to teleport to and from your camp at will (outside combat) is unimmersive
-Movement in combat is buggier than it should be
-Several instances of mechanics or effects are mentioned and never explained, leaving it as an exercise to the reader to attempt to work out what they do (i.e. google it, and hope to avoid spoilers in the process - they show up in the dumbest places)

-Almost all party members are highly good-aligned, leaving you with almost no choices if you want an evil-aligned campaign with members that have a story

Look, I know it's an amazing game. But it's not without its faults. If I'm playing an RPG, what I care about is the narrative. This game has a stellar narrative, but the game design actively resists showing it to you. The narrative allows some choice, but it's mostly built on allowing failure and presenting consequences for failure. Sometimes it's off of a failed dice roll and very often it's based on conversation tree options that vague and don't communicate the weight attached to them. I'm not opposed to meaningful choices or hard choices, but... the way the game allows and punishes failure often leads to worse gameplay and a lower quality narrative than what the game has to offer.

This can be related to small things, like a combat encounter that becomes impossibly hard and frustrating because you missed a character's side conversation, failed a persuasion roll, or didn't realize that it'd be easier if you LET yourself be ambushed. This can be annoying but it's not a dealbreaker.

The dealbreaker is allowing failure on major plot points (losing characters, or even losing companions), then doing nothing to transition the story or character dynamics in response. I'm having to Google if certain things are bugged. The negative consequences often come on suddenly and they aren't followed up with conversations or narrator cues to unpack what happened and what comes next; nothing fills the void of what you missed or lost. I've had to repeatedly save scum and force the "good outcome" just to feel in touch with the narrative. I'll still dump a ton of hours into BG3, but I'll be frustrated for far too many of them.

I first bought Elden Ring in 2022, but despite spending over 200 hours on Steam, I never managed to finish it. Part of the problem was my approach: I relied on walkthroughs that explained almost everything, which made the experience unnecessarily slow and, eventually, boring.

Later, I decided to give the game another chance on PlayStation, this time with a different goal: completing it and collecting all the trophies. That approach worked much better for me. After spending another 100 hours on PlayStation, I finally achieved the Platinum trophy.

Now that I've completed the game, I can confidently say that Elden Ring is a masterpiece. It's beautiful, ambitious, and filled with incredible details. However, even a masterpiece isn't without flaws.

1. An Excessively Large World

Elden Ring's world is enormous, and while exploration is one of its main attractions, its sheer size can become exhausting. Some players may enjoy getting lost and discovering things along the way, but for others, constantly wandering around without a clear sense of direction can become frustrating. I have nothing against open-world Souls games, but I think Elden Ring sometimes takes this concept too far.

2. Overcomplicated Level and Path Design**

In traditional, linear Souls games, finding hidden paths, discovering shortcuts, and struggling to reach a particular item or boss can be a rewarding part of the experience. However, in a massive open world like Elden Ring, this design philosophy can sometimes become more frustrating than enjoyable. The combination of an enormous map and complicated paths doesn't always work in the game's favor.

I feel that FromSoftware struggled to find the right balance between freedom, accessibility, and genuine difficulty, particularly when it comes to boss fights.

The scope of the game is as impressive as it is ambitious; however, the combat system and the way in which the game feels to navigate makes for a grating, miserable experience, no matter how good or bad the decisions are that you make.

The main aspect of combat that makes it feel so terrible is that the enemy uses its infinite well of spell slots, class features, and general knowledge about the game to put you into infuriating lose-lose scenarios with shockingly little variance. Every Single Enemy in the game will make the exact optimal choice -- factoring in ally/enemy positioning and lines of sight, health pools, class capabilities, equipped loadouts, available consumables, environmental hazards, etc. -- which, while technically impressive (and made my high-end computer sound like a goddamn helicopter), really isn't that fun to try and deal with. After a certain point of enemies standing in doorways to block line of sight between allies, it became less of an "our characters versus the enemy characters" experience and more of an immersion-breaking fight of "us versus the game."

Story moments being locked by default for player characters who are unconscious was another glaring downside. Perhaps there are more ways to pick up on the intricacies of what's going on with Baldur's Gate before you get there in a four-player party, but despite our thorough efforts, we weren't able to figure it out.

I did quite appreciate the writing of this game. It was consistently great across the board.
